claims.text: Schwab's 2025 10-K (published February 2026) says that, coupled with scale, its operating efficiency and sharing of infrastructure across businesses creates a cost advantage that lets it competitively price products and services while profitably serving clients of various sizes across multiple channels.

Schwab's 2025 10-K (published February 2026) lists brand and corporate reputation as enabling it to attract clients and employees and to credibly introduce new products. It also says service culture earns trust and loyalty and increases the likelihood that clients refer others. Management also cites its 'Willingness to Disrupt' as helping attract more clients and assets.

On the 1Q25 earnings call (April 2025), the CFO said Schwab's balanced approach to expense management had enabled it to drive expense on client assets down into the low double digits and improve cost per account by more than 20% over the last decade. No per-client acquisition cost is stated in this evidence.

Schwab's 2025 10-K (published February 2026) reports 4.7 million new brokerage accounts in 2025, up 13% from the prior year. Core net new assets were $519.4 billion, a 5.1% annualized organic growth rate, and active brokerage accounts were 38.5 million. The 2024 comparison was 4.2 million new accounts and $366.9 billion of core net new assets.
On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), CEO Rick Wurster said 1.9 million new retail households turned to Schwab in 2025. He said the average new-to-firm retail client is in their 30s.

Schwab's 2Q26 release (July 2026) reports 1.4 million new brokerage accounts, core net new assets of $119.8 billion (up 49% versus 2Q25) and 48.0 million total client accounts. The 3Q26 release (October 2026) reports 1.2 million new brokerage accounts and core net new assets of $190.4 billion (up 38% versus 3Q25).

At its May 2026 investor day, Schwab's marketing presentation described marketing as 'a core growth engine for consistent client & asset growth' and said its 'data & insight-led model drives efficiency at scale'.

On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Wurster listed growth investments: more branches in local communities, more financial consultants, strategic marketing and advertising (including adapting marketing to the increased influence of LLMs), an RIA support ecosystem, and bringing Schwab's breadth to workplace clients. He cited 2.7 million new brokerage accounts in the first half of 2026.

On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), the CFO said Schwab's 2026 spending plan targets new client growth and deeper relationships with individual investors and RIAs, while 'harnessing incremental scale and efficiency'. Examples were investing in branches, adding financial consultants and wealth advisors, advertising and marketing, spot crypto trading, and more AI in service and technology. He said this implies meaningful operating leverage and pre-tax margin expansion into the low 50s.

Advisor Services: on the 4Q25 call (January 2026), Wurster said Schwab attracts net new assets from new and existing advisors of all sizes. Schwab's 2025 10-K describes referrals to independent RIAs through the Schwab Advisor Network. Its investor-day disclosures state that Schwab Advisor Network advisors pay fees to Schwab in connection with referrals. In 3Q26 Schwab announced a partnership with Anthropic to bring Claude for Financial Advisors to the independent RIAs it serves.

claims.text: Workplace: Schwab's 2025 10-K describes Workplace Services (Retirement Plan Services, Retirement Business Services, Stock Plan Services, Designated Brokerage Services). It says Schwab Private Issuer Equity Services was introduced in late 2025. Schwab reported 5.9 million workplace plan participant accounts as of August 31, 2026. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Wurster said the stock plan business has been 'thriving' and that retirement is an area where Schwab 'could be doing more' to introduce itself to many working Americans for the first time. On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), he cited wins in private stock plan administration and increased momentum in retirement plans.

claims.text: Cross-selling and bank: on the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Wurster said clients 'continue turning to Schwab for more of their financial lives'. Managed investing net flows reached a quarterly record of $24 billion and bank lending reached $72 billion, up 35% year-over-year. On the 4Q24 call (January 2025), he described the bank as built for investors, with among the lowest lending rates in the industry and pledged asset lines in a day.

Acquisitions and integration: on the 2Q25 call (July 2025), Wurster said Schwab had gone from losing assets with Ameritrade clients to stable last year and then growth. He said he expected that to accelerate and become a more meaningful part of net new assets. In 1Q26 Schwab closed the Forge Global acquisition in early March, with management saying it will give clients direct and indirect access to pre-IPO company shares. The 2Q26 10-Q reports Forge acquisition and integration costs of $28 million in the quarter and $39 million in the first six months, and expects full-year 2026 expenses excluding interest to rise approximately 10% to 11%.

claims.text: Edward Jones (10-Q, 2Q26, published August 2026): client assets and households are growing slowly. Financial advisors totaled 20,514 at period end, up 1% year-over-year. Net new assets were $18 billion in the quarter and $36 billion in the first half, up 6% in each period.
Edward Jones (10-Q, 1Q26, published May 2026): client households at period end were 6.8 million, up 3%, and net new assets were $18 billion, up 4%.

Edward Jones (10-Q, 3Q25, published November 2025): net new households were 24,000 in the quarter versus 53,000 a year earlier (-55%). For nine months they were 101,000 versus 177,000 (-43%). Client households were 6.7 million, and financial advisors were 20,429 at period end, up 3%.

Edward Jones (10-Q, 2Q25, published August 2025): net new households were 27,000 versus 60,000 a year earlier, and net new assets decreased 10%. The firm said this continued a downward trend attributable to higher asset outflows, which are affected by an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm, macroeconomic volatility, inflation and consumer spending. It also said financial advisor attrition increased to 6.4%, primarily due to more retirements.

Edward Jones (2025 10-K, published March 2026) states that its total households and net new assets goals depend on retaining and growing the number of financial advisors and on advisors' ability to compete for clients. It says competitors are offering guaranteed contracts, upfront payments and increased compensation, which could raise the Partnership's compensation costs and reduce profitability. It also says slower talent growth could mean slower growth in client accounts and net new assets.

Edward Jones (10-Q, 1Q26, published May 2026) reports that financial advisor compensation increased 13% to $1,875 in the quarter, primarily due to higher revenues on which commissions are earned. Variable compensation increased 22% to $748.

Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (published March 2026) says the Partnership is making substantial investments in initiatives that include High Net Worth; Workplace, which connects local business owners and their employees with financial solutions through their workplace; and a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors. It adds that it cannot reliably predict the timing or outcome of these initiatives and that their success depends on broad adoption by advisors and associates.

Edward Jones's 2025 10-K describes a Digital and Data division that supports significant investment in technology infrastructure and digital initiatives. The 10-K says this provides new tools for branch teams and operational efficiencies that reduce manual processes. The 10-K also names competitive pressure from digital experiences, AI and lower-cost computer-based 'robo-advice', which it says is driving significant investment in technology infrastructure, digital initiatives and strategic relationships.

Edward Jones's 10-Qs (2025-2026) describe 'Enterprise Reimagined', which the firm says will create more efficient operations by restructuring and reducing the size of the home office, removing redundancies, and adopting new capabilities, processes and technology. It frames this under a strategic ambition to improve the financial wellness of tens of millions of long-term investors across North America. In 3Q25 communications and data processing expense increased 23% to $300, and in 2Q26 the firm again cited continued investments in new tools and technology.

Edward Jones reported income before allocations margin of 12.0% in 2Q26 and 11.7% for 1H26. The firm describes its margin as 'a strategic balance between investing in the future and current financial results'.

The evidence above only provides objective context for the strategic question asked. Whether or how Edward Jones should act is a judgment for the strategy team to make, beyond the scope of this evidence engine.

claims.text: On the 4Q24 earnings call (January 2025), the CFO described the conversion as "channel migration": Workplace assets that began in Workplace move into the advisor-led channel. She said that since 2020 the firm has seen $300 billion coming and initiating at some point from Workplace and moving into the advisor-led channel. She said the earlier focus on companion accounts, from the E*TRADE and Morgan Stanley platform integration, was largely complete.

On the 1Q25 call (April 2025), the CFO cited assets migrating to the advisor-led channel that originated in workplace, "with an incremental $20 billion this quarter, adding to the roughly $300 billion accumulated from workplace since we expanded our channel in 2020."

On the 2Q25 call (July 2025), the CFO said new flows from workplace go into the advisor-led channel and also become fee-based flows. She said 70% of the flows that originate from workplace are net new assets to the firm.

On the 3Q25 call (October 2025), the CFO said assets that originated from workplace continue to migrate into the advisor-led channel because of the firm's platform investments. She said IPO momentum leads people to drop assets into self-directed accounts and also to move them directly into advisor-led accounts. She also described an AI-powered lead distribution platform, LeadIQ, that matches workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitates engagement with financial advisors.

On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), management said advisor-led assets originating from workplace and E*TRADE relationships reached a record $99 billion for the full year, "compared to historical averages of around $60 billion per year." The January 2026 strategic-update deck notes define these as assets brought into advisor-led relationships where the initial account was workplace or self-directed, averaged across 2020–2024.

On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), the CFO described the funnel as a first step of retaining vested assets: Workplace showed greater retention of assets that vested, which translated into NNA. The second step is channel migration, where workplace assets seek advice. She said that migration has helped contribute to over $1 trillion of total assets in the adviser-led strategy.

On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), the CFO said net new assets were a record $148 billion. Stock plan IPO flows were just over half of that, which she said illustrates the workplace channel as "a strong contributor to the top of the funnel." She said "Workplace brings relationships and assets onto the platform." Asked about new versus existing clients, she said the mix includes new and existing accounts, and that for those without an advice relationship "we're working on that referral model." She said that model can begin as early as financial education and cited 401(k) examples.

On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), the CFO said IPO-related flows were again just over half of NNA. She said "our pipeline and our connectivity across channels allows us to build relationships early and deepen them over time." CEO Ted Pick said the attachment points bring clients to E*TRADE and keep the firm close to them in the corporate stock plan context, and that where appropriate fee-based flows make their way to the advisers. He also said lockups expiring and fund distributions create further opportunities to retain assets.

In the 3Q26 call (October 2026), the CFO said fee-based flows can come from a corporate retirement mandate. She said backlogs of dollars accumulated in brokerage (advisory and self-directed) then moved into fee-based flows, and that stock plan relationships can aggregate assets and move them directly into fee-based.
Baseline (supplement for 4Q20, published January 2021): workplace unvested assets were $435 billion and the number of participants was 4,885 (000's).

The 2025 10-K (published February 2026) reports stock plan unvested assets of $534 billion at December 31, 2025 versus $475 billion at December 31, 2024. Participants were 6.5 million versus 6.6 million. Management attributes the slight 2025 decline in participants primarily to the disposition of the EMEA stock plan business.

The 2Q26 10-Q (published August 2026) reports stock plan unvested public assets of $658 billion at June 30, 2026, versus $534 billion at December 31, 2025. Stock plan participants were 6.6 million, versus 6.5 million. The filing states these unvested assets are not included in client assets and exclude private company securities. Participants are counted in each plan, so individuals in multiple plans are counted more than once.

The 3Q26 supplement (published October 2026) shows stock plan unvested public assets of $638 billion at September 30, 2026, versus $658 billion at June 30, 2026 and $534 billion at September 30, 2025.
claims.source_label: MS supplement - Wealth Management segment 2026-09-30, p.8 [IR]

claims.text: The January 2026 strategic-update deck defines "Workplace Participants" as Stock Plan, Institutional Consulting, and Retirement and Financial Wellness participants, excluding overlap. It defines Core Client Relationships as Advisor-Led Households, Self-Directed Households and Workplace Participants, excluding overlap. The deck shows core client relationships of ~13 million in 2020 and ~20 million in 2025.

On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), CEO Ted Pick said Morgan Stanley at Work, with its exclusive partnership with Carta, positions the firm as an early trusted advisor to over 50,000 private companies. He said employees across workplace companies benefit from equity compensation plan management, liquidity opportunities and full-service advice.

The January 2026 strategic-update deck lays out the corporate and employee offering across the company life cycle:
- Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits
- Founders Wealth Strategies
- Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation
- Private Shares Trading & Lending
- IPO Execution and Support Services
- MS at Work stock plan and 401k, cap table management, and cash management solutions
- Private capital markets, tenders and financing

On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), the CFO said the firm has about 70% of the top 100 unicorns by market cap in its workplace pipeline. She described IPOs as a form of "top of the funnel" NNA, and a referral model that can begin at the financial education stage and with 401(k) assets.

On the 2Q25 call (July 2025), the CFO tied self-directed flows to marketing and business development investments and new tools such as E*TRADE Pro. On the 3Q25 call (October 2025), she cited the launch of Power eTrade Pro. On the 4Q24 call (January 2025), she said the Carta partnership puts the firm at the center of new stock plan opportunities as private companies consider going public.
claims.source_label: MS transcript 2025-06-30 [IR]; MS transcript 2025-09-30 [IR]; MS transcript 2024-12-31 [IR]

claims.text: The 2Q26 10-Q (published August 2026) describes the Wealth Management offering as spanning advisor-led brokerage, cash management, financial and wealth planning, workplace services including stock plan administration, securities-based lending, residential and commercial real estate loans, banking and retirement plan services. The filing does not break out workplace-specific lending or cash management results.

The January 2026 strategic-update deck presents firmwide goals of WM pre-tax margin 30% and client assets $10 trillion+. It notes that the attainment of these objectives assumes a normal market environment and may be impacted by external factors including geopolitical, macroeconomic and market conditions and legislation and regulation.

On the 4Q24 call (January 2025), CEO Ted Pick said the KPI is whether the firm is "increasing the TAM of relationships" through the financial advisory lever, Workplace and self-directed, and then how fee-based flows are developing.

On the 1Q25 call (April 2025), the CFO said workplace is "a little bit less in our control" and named it as the vulnerability in a downturn: stock grants and vesting could decrease and there might not be IPO events.

The 2025 10-K (published February 2026) says Wealth Management competes across advisor-led, workplace and digital direct channels. It says competitive ability is affected by brand and reputation, the breadth, depth and pricing of product offerings, and technology supporting evolving client needs, including generative AI and tokenization.

The 2Q26 10-Q (published August 2026) states that NNA levels are influenced by seasonality, the firm's ability to attract and retain advisors and clients, capital market and corporate activities that may affect assets in certain channels, and large idiosyncratic inflows and outflows. It adds that "Should these factors continue, the growth rate of our NNA may be impacted."

On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), the CFO said flows will fluctuate as lockups expire, funds make distributions and individuals use assets for consumption. CEO Ted Pick said NNA "will ebb and flow in a given quarter," while management believes the workplace cycle "has many years to come."

adjacent.text: InvestmentNews trade press (2026-09-16) says Morgan Stanley's wealth division reported workplace participants up 2% from the previous year, with self-directed households up 5%, and cites the firm as saying more than half of the NNA is tied to IPO-related flows.

claims.text: The firm's 2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says it offers multiple affiliation options, which it calls AdvisorChoice®. Advisors primarily affiliate directly as employees or independent contractors, or as employees of third-party RIAs and broker-dealers served through the RIA and Custody Services (RCS) division.

Employee advisors, per the 2025 10-K, work in a traditional branch supported by local management and administrative staff and serve predominantly retail clients. Their compensation primarily includes a payout on revenues they generate, and they participate in the firm's employee benefit plans.

Independent contractor advisors, per the 2025 10-K, are generally responsible for all their direct costs and so receive a higher payout percentage than employee advisors. The firm describes these options as designed to let advisors use as much or as little of its support as they choose. They may affiliate directly or through an affiliated bank or credit union in the Financial Institutions Division.

The Raymond James affiliation-options web page (page content as of 2026-04-21) lists five AdvisorChoice options: Traditional Employee, Advisor Select, Independent Contractor, Bank & Credit Union, and Corporate RIA. It also lists RIA & Custody Services as a model. Qualification thresholds differ: for example, Traditional Employee needs a minimum of 5 years of experience, and Independent Contractor needs a minimum of 3 years and a minimum T12 of $150,000 to join an existing branch or $400,000 to open a new one.
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-04-21 [IR]

claims.text: The recruiting page for Advisor Select (page content as of 2026-03-11) describes it as an employee affiliation option. Established advisors get the employee channel's benefits and create their own branches, running the branch's P&L to earn a higher rate on production. The affiliation-options page (as of 2026-04-21) lists a minimum of 3 years of experience and $3.5 million or higher in annual branch fees and commission revenue.
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-03-11 [IR]; RJF press page content as of 2026-04-21 [IR]

claims.text: The affiliation-options page (as of 2026-04-21) lists thresholds for the remaining models. Bank & Credit Union requires a minimum of 3 years and $250,000 in production. Corporate RIA requires a minimum of 3 years and $50 million in assets under advisement. RIA & Custody Services requires $100 million or more to establish a new RIA, a minimum of $30 million to plug in an existing RIA, and $1 billion or more in assets under management for introducing broker/dealers. In RCS, the advisor is responsible for compliance.
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-04-21 [IR]

claims.text: In RCS, per the 2025 10-K, third-party RIAs and broker-dealers receive custodial services, trade execution, research and other support. Those firms retain the fees they charge their clients and are generally responsible for their own direct costs. RCS advisors are not in the firm's financial advisor counts, although their client assets are in AUA. RCS AUA was $217.3 billion as of September 30, 2025.

The 10-Q for the period ended 2026-06-30 (published 2026-08-05) shows RCS assets of $251.3 billion as of June 30, 2026, of which $220.1 billion were in fee-based accounts. It says RCS growth is partially due to transfers into RCS from the firm's other advisor channels, which it does not expect to significantly affect results of operations.

Payout - Employee and Advisor Select (page content as of 2026-04-21): Traditional Employee is listed at up to 50% payout with a full array of employee benefits. Advisor Select is listed at 70-80% gross payout with employee benefits.
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-04-21 [IR]

claims.text: Payout - Independent Contractor and Corporate RIA (page content as of 2026-04-21): both are listed at 81% to 90% payout, with benefits built through third-party partnerships. Bank & Credit Union advisors receive a compensation package from the financial institution in partnership with Raymond James. For RIA & Custody Services, the RIA or broker/dealer determines compensation with the advisor and creates its own benefits.
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-04-21 [IR]

claims.text: The 2025 10-K says employee advisors' compensation primarily includes a payout on revenues they generate. Independent contractors bear their own direct costs and so receive a higher payout percentage. This is the structural basis for the payout differences in the published ranges.

Firm revenue - RCS: the 2025 10-K says the firm receives fees from RCS clients that may be transactional or based on AUA. The 10-Q (period ended 2026-06-30) says revenues related to RCS assets in the PCG segment are included in "Account and service fees".
claims.source_label: RJF 10-K - Private Client Group segment 2025-09-30 [filing]; RJF 10-Q 2026-06-30 [filing]

claims.text: Firm revenue - PCG overall: the 2025 10-K says segment revenues are typically driven by AUA and are generally asset-based or transactional. It lists RJBDP sweep fees from third-party banks and from the firm's Bank segment, plus client account fees. Those account fees include custodial, trade execution, research and support services for third-party RIAs and broker-dealers through RCS.

The 10-Q for the period ended 2026-03-31 (published 2026-05-06) says most fee-based PCG assets are in programs where the firm's advisors provide advisory services. Administrative services are generally performed by the Asset Management segment, so a portion of the related revenue is shared with that segment. It adds that a significant portion of PCG revenues is directly impacted by market movements.

Margin effect: the 10-Q (period ended 2026-03-31) attributes a 3% decrease in PCG pre-tax income for the quarter to a higher proportion of compensable revenues to total net revenues, resulting from lower interest-related revenues. On the call published 2026-01-28, the CFO said interest rate reductions reduced the segment's non-compensable revenues.

Recruiting cost: on the call published 2025-10-22, the CFO said fiscal 2025 adjusted compensation expense included $355 million of amortization of transition assistance for recruited advisors and other retention awards to existing advisors, up approximately 11% versus fiscal 2024. The firm's supplement (published 2026-07-22) shows recruiting and retention-related compensation of $117 million in the quarter ended June 30, 2026 and $335 million for the nine months, up 22%. The firm says such awards are expensed over the requisite service period, typically between 5 and 10 years.
claims.source_label: RJF transcript 2025-09-30 [IR]; RJF supplement 2026-06-30, p.6 [IR]; RJF supplement 2026-06-30, p.18 [IR]

claims.text: Management commentary on transition assistance: on the call published 2025-01-29, Shoukry said that as production grows there is a scale advantage because transition-assistance amortization is not growing as fast as fee-based revenue. On the call published 2026-04-22, he said the firm now breaks out recruiting and retention cost for transparency. He said it prefers recruiting one by one to acquisitions because 100% of the transition assistance goes to retention of the advisor.

Recruiting results - fiscal 2025 (call published 2025-10-22): Shoukry reported record recruiting into the domestic independent contractor and employee channels, with $407 million of trailing-12-month production, a 21% increase over the prior record. The recruited advisors had approximately $58 billion of client assets at their previous firms. Including RCS, total recruited client assets were nearly $63 billion across all platforms. He said the success was broad-based across the employee, independent contractor and RCS channels.

Recruiting results - later quarters. Call published 2026-01-28: trailing-12-month recruited production of nearly $460 million and over $63 billion of client assets, or more than $69 billion including RCS. Call published 2026-04-22: $141 million and nearly $21 billion in the quarter, which he called the second highest quarterly result in the firm's history. Call published 2026-07-22: $156 million and nearly $23 billion in the quarter.
claims.source_label: RJF transcript 2025-12-31 [IR]; RJF transcript 2026-03-31 [IR]; RJF transcript 2026-06-30 [IR]

claims.text: Channel mix: on the call published 2026-01-28, Shoukry said recruiting is broad-based across the affiliation options, maybe more heavily tilted toward the independent contractor side in the last six months. On the call published 2026-07-22, he said the pipeline is not driven by one firm, catalyst or affiliation option and that fiscal year-to-date net new assets of $75 billion were up 119%. A trade-press report published 2026-11-05 says he described the independent contractor division as seeing the most interest by dollar volume.
claims.source_label: RJF transcript 2025-12-31 [IR]; RJF transcript 2026-06-30 [IR]; RJF trade 2026-11-05 [trade press (indicative only)]

claims.text: Retention and headcount: on the call published 2025-10-22, Shoukry said the firm ended the fiscal year with a record number of advisors, 2% higher than the prior year. The 2025 10-K says advisor numbers rose because recruits and trainees moved into production roles exceeded departures and planned retirements. On the call published 2026-07-22, Shoukry cited a 97% adviser satisfaction rate and said retention is the foundation for growth.

Retention setback and risks: the firm cited the departure of primarily one large branch in its independent contractor division in fiscal Q1 2025, roughly $5 billion of AUA, as a drag on net new assets. The 2025 10-K also names an industry-wide trend of advisors leaving traditional firms for independent RIAs, including some backed by private equity. It says this makes recruiting highly competitive and that continued departures, including to an unaffiliated RIA channel, could adversely affect PCG. It lists succession planning and a broad range of services as mitigants.

Strategy and value proposition: on the calls published 2025-07-23 and 2026-01-28, Shoukry described a "best of both worlds" value proposition, combining an advisor- and client-focused culture with leading technology and solutions. He said it resonates across all affiliation options, and that the strong balance sheet and commitment to independence are differentiators. On the call published 2026-07-22, he said the firm has the largest addressable market because it offers all the affiliation options an advisor could want. He said the firm is indifferent to how advisors affiliate and wants them to fall in love with the culture, values and platform.
claims.source_label: RJF transcript 2025-06-30 [IR]; RJF transcript 2025-12-31 [IR]; RJF transcript 2026-06-30 [IR]

claims.text: Competitive positioning: on the call published 2025-10-22, Shoukry said the firm focuses on the long term and a stable platform whereas many competitors look for an exit in three to five years or less. He also said many competitors compete with the largest check and change comp plans every year to cross-sell more bank products. On the call published 2026-01-28, he said the firm has critical mass and decades of experience in each of the employee, independent contractor and RIA custody options, and is not testing a new venture. The 2025 10-K separately lists competition from national broker-dealers, banks, investment advisors and fintechs.

Shared platform and technology: on the call published 2026-01-28, Shoukry said the firm has been investing close to $1.1 billion in technology and AI. He said competitors with similar cultures invest a fraction of that. He cited the private wealth advisor program, an expanded alternatives platform, and a newly launched proprietary digital AI operations agent named Rai. On the call published 2026-07-22, he again cited $1.1 billion of technology investment and said AI will differentiate firms and extend the platform.

The recruiting pages (content as of 2026-05-19, 2026-05-17 and 2026-07-12) describe a common platform behind each option. Independent contractors get a full-service, self-clearing NYSE-member broker/dealer with investing, planning, private wealth, marketing and technology. Bank and credit union advisors get the full Raymond James wealth platform, technology and home office team. RCS firms get an integrated platform with flexibility to add third-party applications, plus transitions management, practice management and recruiting assistance.
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-05-19 [IR]; RJF press page content as of 2026-05-17 [IR]; RJF press page content as of 2026-07-12 [IR]

claims.text: Platform liability: the 2025 10-K notes that the firm provides custody, clearing and back-office support to non-affiliated independent RIAs and broker-dealers. Those firms are exclusively responsible for their own operations, supervision and compliance, but the firm has been and may be named as a defendant in litigation involving their clients.

adjacent.text: The call published 2026-07-22 reports PCG pre-tax income of $423 million on record quarterly net revenues of $2.84 billion for the whole segment. It attributes the growth to higher PCG AUA and says investments in growth, including record recruiting results, partly offset it.
adjacent.differs_because: This is segment-level PCG revenue and profit across all channels combined, not revenue or margin for each affiliation option.

adjacent.text: The firm's supplement (published 2026-07-22) shows total financial advisor compensation of $1,683 million in the quarter ended June 30, 2026, and $4,967 million for the nine months.
adjacent.differs_because: Aggregate compensation expense covers all employees and pay types; it is not the advisor payout grid.

gaps.what: Revenue and margin by affiliation option (employee, independent contractor, RCS) are not disclosed. The firm reports PCG as one segment and shows only RCS assets and the revenue line RCS fees map to ("Account and service fees").
gaps.suggested_source: Investor-day or segment disclosure breaking out PCG revenue and pre-tax margin by channel; management commentary on channel economics

gaps.what: Headline payout ranges are published (company recruiting page, as of 2026-04-21); the full payout grid is not public.

claims.text: Schwab (2025 10-K, published 2026-02-25): net revenues were $23.9 billion in 2025. Net interest revenue was $11.8 billion, asset management and administration fees $6.5 billion, trading revenue $3.9 billion, and bank deposit account fee revenue $977 million. Schwab ties net interest revenue to lower funding costs and growth in margin and bank lending. It ties asset management and administration fees to higher client asset balances, and trading revenue to higher trading volume.

claims.text: Position: digital-first, AI-assisted advice becomes the expectation. A Wealthtender study (published 2025-08-13) anticipates continued growth in AI tool use for advisor searches, rising expectations for faster response times and digital-first communications, and further acceptance of virtual advisor relationships regardless of geography. It says the pattern of higher comfort with AI for administrative and analytical tasks than for autonomous decision-making is likely to remain consistent.

Position: AI changes advisor capacity and workflows, with the client still dealing with a human. Deloitte (article, 2026-05-20) says advisers spend nearly 70% of their time on behind-the-scenes work. It predicts adviser productivity uplift of roughly 30% to 100% by 2032 from agentic AI, and says this could shift the issue from adviser scarcity to adviser capability.

Position: AI is widely expected to be transformative. In Accenture research (published 2025-06-23), 97% say AI will have a transformative effect on the future of financial advice to a moderate or great extent in the next three years. 55% say AI will be most helpful in eliminating administrative tasks, identifying next best action opportunities, and automating marketing and client contact. 47% believe AI will have a direct, measurable and consistent impact on the client-adviser relationship in the next 12 months.

Position: AI will take over tasks but not the core advice relationship. McKinsey (published 2026-04-08) says AI will aggressively assume specific tasks such as preparation, data extraction and document drafting. It calls the replacement thesis "mostly false" for core advice segments, where nearly 80 percent of affluent households still prefer a human relationship. It adds that an AI takeover might be possible for standardized, lower-touch service models and for younger clients, who are increasingly comfortable with AI-only interfaces.

Position: AI changes how clients interact with advice, but they still prefer a human. In the Bank of America Private Bank 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (published 2026-06-17), 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets and 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios. Yet 65% still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor. A Wealthtender study (2025-08-13) found respondents comfortable with AI for admin tasks, somewhat comfortable with AI helping generate personalized financial plans, and uncomfortable with investment decisions outsourced to AI.

Firm view (Raymond James): on the 2Q26 call (published 2026-07-22), CEO Paul Shoukry said the firm's culture and trusted relationships "can't be replicated by AI or technology, but it will be helped by AI and technology". Management said it will keep investing in the people, platforms and capabilities that help its financial professionals deliver more holistic and personalized advice. It also cited more than $1.1 billion in annual technology spend, including automation, process improvement and AI, to equip advisers with private wealth tools to deliver deeper, more tailored advice while keeping personal relationships at the center. On the 1Q26 call (2026-04-22), Shoukry said that in a world being shaped by AI, technology and constant change, "personal relationships will matter more, not less."

Firm view (Schwab): on the 1Q26 call (published 2026-04-16), CEO Rick Wurster said AI "opens up new distribution channels and allows us to create personalized relationships with clients we have not been able to serve with a person-to-person relationship." Schwab's 3Q26 press release (2026-10-15) lists Charley, a new AI-powered assistant giving U.S. retail clients conversational access to Schwab's tools and insights, and a partnership with Anthropic to bring Claude for Financial Advisors to independent RIAs. The 2Q26 release (2026-07-21) describes Portfolio Insights, a generative AI feature, and carries the caveat that it should not be construed as investment advice.
claims.source_label: SCHW transcript 2026-03-31 [IR]; SCHW press 2026-09-30 [filing]; SCHW press 2026-06-30 [filing]

claims.text: Firm view (Bank of America / Merrill): on the 3Q26 call (published 2026-10-14), CFO Alastair Borthwick said advisor productivity, disciplined pricing, digital engagement and AI tools "continue to expand our capacity to deliver personalized advice at scale". The 3Q26 earnings release for the GWIM segment lists, under Merrill Wealth Management, 87% of Merrill households digitally active, 70K digital appointments scheduled in the quarter and 81% of eligible brokerage and bank accounts opened through digital onboarding.
claims.source_label: BAC transcript - GWIM segment 2026-09-30 [IR]; BAC press - GWIM segment 2026-09-30 [filing]

claims.text: Firm view (Edward Jones): its 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says the industry is evolving technologically, with more firms offering personalized services and enhanced digital experiences, including AI and lower-cost computer-based "robo-advice". It names Financial Planning Services, where clients get a more personalized experience with additional planning capabilities, and a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors. It says it cannot reliably predict the timing or outcome of these initiatives. A trade report (2026-08-18) says Edward Jones took a minority stake in Quicken, with the stated intention of integrating personal financial management more directly into advisor conversations; the report notes the deployment strategy is still being determined.

Position: advice becomes more holistic, and the relationship manager becomes an orchestrator. Capgemini's World Wealth Report 2026 (published 2026-06-03) sets out a readiness-led sequence from now to later. It describes shifting towards AI-augmented advisory orchestration, embedding planning across major life events, enabling proactive, insight-led advice, and later moving towards autonomous, tailored portfolio delivery. It says advisory roles and incentive structures are redefined so RMs orchestrate experiences across the wealth ecosystem, coordinating specialists in tax, estate planning, lending, philanthropy and non-financial services, and that some organizational resistance will be inevitable. It reports that 60% of executives say their firm lacks a unified client view and that 42% of HNWIs have to restate their goals and preferences multiple times to the same firm.
claims.source_label: Research research 2026-06-03, p.46 [research]; Research research 2026-06-03, p.19 [research]

claims.text: Position: clients want planning and broader life guidance, not just investments. Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published 2025-10-09) says wealthy Gen X, Y and Z investors are reshaping the advisor-client relationship with a focus on holistic financial planning and life goal achievement. They seek transparency in advisor compensation and broader life guidance beyond investment management. McKinsey (2026-04-08) says its research shows interest in holistic advice rose from 29 percent in 2018 to 52 percent in 2023. In a Wealthtender survey (2025-08-13), 49.00% of respondents named helping them plan for long-term goals as the most valuable advisor role, and 34.00% named providing expert investment advice.
claims.source_label: Research research 2025-10-09 [research]; Research research 2026-04-08, p.3 [research]; Research research 2025-08-13 [research]

claims.text: Position: fee models will likely stay plural, with pricing open to change. Cerulli (published 2025-05-28) finds 33% of affluent investors pay through an asset-based fee versus 36% who prefer it, 21% use a no-fee platform and 20% a commission-based method. It cautions firms not to limit themselves to one engagement option. On the 1Q26 call (published 2026-04-22), Raymond James's CEO said the firm wants a "profitable and competitive and fair pricing structure" and would be "flexible and open to evolving" if the industry and client preferences move; he said the firm reviews fees and payout on an ongoing basis.

Firm view (Edward Jones): its 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) describes a branch model built on deep personal relationships and comprehensive advice and planning. Its Guided Solutions program has advisors guide clients through a required process of identifying financial goals and selecting a portfolio objective.

Firm view (Bank of America): its November 2025 investor day deck (published 2025-11-05) segments wealth clients by tier. It lists a predominantly digital experience for Mass Market (<$500K) and goals-based advice, described as "guidance delivered at scale", for Mass Affluent ($500K-$1MM). It lists dedicated advice and customizable solutions for complex needs for High Net Worth ($1MM-$10MM).

Position: the mass-affluent and middle market are the next frontier for advice. Cerulli (published 2026-03-25) says middle-market and mass-affluent households with $100,000 to $2 million in financial assets hold $25 trillion across 46.9 million households. It describes them as typically younger and less advised, seeking involved advisor relationships, and says this will benefit providers that can offer streamlined advisory services at scale. It notes firms have traditionally started relationships only after prospects reach minimums of $250,000 to more than $1 million.

Position: remote and virtual access is becoming acceptable. Wealthtender (published 2025-08-13) reports that a third of respondents said an advisor's location is not a factor because they prefer to meet exclusively online. It also anticipates further acceptance of virtual advisor relationships regardless of geographic location. Schwab's 10-K (2026-02-25) describes advisory solutions with minimum investments starting at $5,000, alongside self-directed digital platforms.
claims.source_label: Research research 2025-08-13 [research]; SCHW 10-K - Investor Services segment 2025-12-31 [filing]

claims.text: Position: younger clients reach advice through different channels and want more control. On the 3Q25 call (published 2025-10-16), Schwab's CEO said nearly one-third of new-to-firm retail households this year are Gen Zers, who learn about finances primarily through social media and family. Cerulli (2025-10-29) says younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives. Schwab's investor-day grid (2026-05-14) maps self-direct investors, younger investors, advice seekers and H/UHNW to different channels.
claims.source_label: SCHW transcript 2025-09-30 [IR]; Research research 2025-10-29, p.2 [research]; SCHW deck 2026-05-14, p.63 [IR]

claims.text: Firm view (Schwab): on the 3Q26 call (published 2026-10-15), CEO Wurster said Schwab has approximately 2% of the $37 trillion U.S. advice market. He said only about 5% of Schwab retail households currently use an advice solution, while 31% say they are willing to pay for advice.

Firm view (Morgan Stanley): its 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-19) says it competes across advisor-led, workplace and digital direct channels, including on technology such as generative AI and tokenization. Its 3Q26 supplement (2026-10-14) reports separate advisor-led, self-directed and workplace channels, with 8.8 million self-directed households.
claims.source_label: MS 10-K 2025-12-31 [filing]; MS supplement - Wealth Management segment 2026-09-30, p.8 [IR]

claims.text: Firm view (Edward Jones): its 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) lists new-client initiatives. These are High Net Worth, Workplace (connecting local business owners and their employees with financial solutions) and a new digital platform for Next Generation investors. It cites generational wealth transfer and changing client demographics, preferences and values as risks to its model.

gaps.what: How advisor roles and compensation will shift is not forecast in the evidence for most firms. Only Capgemini's generic description of redefined roles and incentives, and Raymond James's statement that it is open to evolving pricing, are available. No firm discloses planned changes to advisor payout or its own fee model.

claims.text: Schwab, 1Q26 call (April 2026): CEO Richard Wurster said Schwab "is already an AI-enabled company." He said AI "opens up new distribution channels and allows us to create personalized relationships with clients we have not been able to serve with a person-to-person relationship."

Schwab, 2Q26 results release (July 2026): Schwab introduced Portfolio Insights, which it calls a generative AI-powered capability that helps investors understand portfolio performance. Its footnote says it gives a narrative snapshot of daily portfolio change, news on top equity movers and Schwab expert content. The same footnote says Insights "should not be construed as investment advice or recommendations" and that generative AI output "may be inaccurate."

Schwab, 3Q26 results release (October 2026): Schwab said it introduced Charley, "a new AI-powered assistant that provides U.S. retail clients with conversational access to Schwab's tools and insights." It also said it partnered with Anthropic to bring Claude for Financial Advisors to the independent RIAs it serves.

Raymond James, 4Q25 call (January 2026): CEO Paul Shoukry said the firm's AI-based tools are "focused on empowering financial advisors and professionals" by applying AI "to enhance service models." He cited the newly launched proprietary digital AI operations agent Rai, which he said builds on a "service-focused, long-term AI strategy."

Morgan Stanley, 3Q25 call (October 2025): the CFO said early AI use cases, "some live and some in pilot," are showing progress. The examples were DevGen AI (developer efficiency), Parable (data analysis and summaries) and LeadIQ, an AI-powered lead distribution platform meant to match workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitate engagement with financial advisors.

Bank of America, GWIM segment commentary (2Q26 call, July 2026): the CFO said the franchise benefited from "new AI-enabled tools that help advisers prepare for client conversations, identify opportunities and deliver more personalized advice at scale." On the 3Q26 call (October 2026) he again named "AI tools" among the factors expanding capacity to deliver personalized advice at scale. These statements are for GWIM, which includes Merrill and the Private Bank.
claims.source_label: BAC transcript - GWIM segment 2026-06-30 [IR]; BAC transcript - GWIM segment 2026-09-30 [IR]

claims.text: Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 study (published June 2026) says the Private Bank uses AI "to support advisor capacity, deepen client relationships, and help teams find information faster and more efficiently."

Capgemini research (published June 2026) sets out a three-horizon roadmap in which the "Later" horizon includes "autonomous portfolio delivery" and AI-enabled estate and tax planning embedded in client journeys. This is a research firm's framing, not a firm's own claim.

Bank of America, 2Q26 call (July 2026): Chairman and CEO Brian Moynihan said over 200,000 teammates use AI-enabled capabilities and generate "more than 400,000 prompts a day." He said "over 300 AI use cases" were approved, of which 114 are live generative AI use cases and 34 are fully implemented. He said the tools are designed to help customer relationship managers "prepare more thoroughly for the client meetings." This is a company-wide statement, not advisor-specific.
Bank of America investor day deck (November 2025): lists an "AI-powered digital assistant for teammates" and "100% of Private Bank teammates with access to AI tools" under team productivity.

Raymond James investor day deck (June 2025): its advisor materials list "Zoom AI Meeting Summaries," GenAI Search and Microsoft CoPilot. Its AI framework includes "Empower Advisors: Integrate AI tools into our advisor platform that reduce the administrative workload."

Raymond James, fiscal 2Q26 release (April 2026): Shoukry said the firm is "increasing AI integration to improve efficiency and provide our financial professionals with more time to serve their clients."

Raymond James, 3Q26 call (July 2026): Shoukry said Raimond, a large language model that answers questions about client accounts, was fully rolled out on June 15 and already had "6,500 unique users" with a "99.5%" satisfaction rate. He also said "close to 20,000" people had completed the four-course module in the firm's AI academy.

Morgan Stanley, 1Q26 call (April 2026): CEO Ted Pick said AI is moving from "pure efficiency exercises" toward "a productivity phenomenon." He described "co-piloting" in which the financial adviser has the historical context of past client interactions, and said the wealth business is working on "super agents" to drive efficiency and effectiveness.

Schwab, 3Q26 call (October 2026): Wurster said Schwab is "simplifying and automating work" so that "a powerful combination of our people and technology can support more clients." Schwab's 3Q26 deck lists a Relationship Management Assistant and workflow automation under "Supercharging Our People & Processes."

McKinsey (published February 2025) estimates that 30 to 40 percent average advisor adoption of wealth-specific gen-AI tools by 2034 "can deliver 6 to 12 percent of time savings." It names meeting preparation and post-meeting notes turned into CRM-integrated summaries as areas of outsize impact.

Deloitte (published May 2026) says advisers spend "nearly 70%" of their time on behind-the-scenes work. It predicts adviser productivity uplift "could reach roughly 30% to 100% by 2032." It also cites industry estimates that 73% of advisory firms use AI in some capacity, only 6% use agentic tools and 5% have implemented cross-system AI integration.

Wealthtender consumer survey (published August 2025): 74% of respondents were comfortable with AI recording and transcribing meetings for note-taking, and 74% with AI drafting routine client communications such as email summaries.

Bank of America, 3Q26 results release (October 2026): the release says "more than 200,000 teammates using AI tools and 300-plus approved use cases across the company, we are turning our scale into a competitive advantage." This is the most explicit competitive-advantage claim with figures in the evidence, and it covers the whole company, not advice only.
Bank of America, 2Q26 call and deck (July 2026): "over 300 AI use cases approved, all of which have good economics," with 114 live generative AI use cases and 34 fully deployed.

Raymond James, 3Q26 call (July 2026): the advisor-facing adoption figures are 6,500 unique users of Raimond within about a month of rollout, a 99.5% satisfaction rate and close to 20,000 people completing its AI academy. Shoukry said AI makes the firm "more confident that a lot of our smaller competitors aren't going to be able to keep up with the level of investment," so "the moat in our industry will increase."

Schwab, 3Q26 call (October 2026): Wurster said "we've already seen developer productivity increase by about 25%." He said Schwab's combination of people, technology, scale and value is "a powerful advantage and one that is very difficult to replicate." Schwab's deck says "AI amplifies our platform advantage." The one quantified result is for developers, not advice.

Morgan Stanley, 3Q26 call (October 2026): the CFO said the firm's scale "supports continued investment in future technology, including AI and digital tools," and that its strengths provide "a powerful competitive advantage." On the 4Q25 call (January 2026) Pick said "our confidence continues to increase in the potential for both the efficiency and the effectiveness of AI-related technologies." No AI results figures appear in these chunks.

Deloitte (published May 2026) estimates AI-driven adviser capacity could equal "US$10 trillion to US$35 trillion in additional client assets" at industry level. It reports that only 6% of advisory firms use agentic tools. These are research estimates, not firm claims.

Raymond James, 3Q26 call (July 2026): in response to an analyst question on whether AI could disrupt advisers or industry economics, Shoukry said "the moat in our industry will increase because ... the cost of making those investments will increase." He said the firm "could not be more optimistic about the future."

Schwab, 2Q26 call (July 2026): Wurster said "there is a bull market for advice" and that retail clients seek holistic advice "through a combination of people and increasingly AI-enabled technology." On the 3Q26 call (October 2026) he described "our people and AI working together to deliver better outcomes for clients."

Edward Jones, 2025 10-K (March 2026): the Partnership says the industry has "an increasing number of firms of all sizes providing personalized services and enhanced digital experiences for clients, including the utilization of artificial intelligence technologies and lower cost, computer-based 'robo-advice'." It says it is also subject to competition from robo-advisors and fintechs, and that if it is "unable to keep pace" with change, including AI changes, it "could lose clients."

Edward Jones, 2025 10-K (March 2026): it lists technology and artificial intelligence among its strategic risks. It says use of AI by the Partnership or its third parties "may expose the Partnership to additional information security and legal risk, increased regulation and regulatory scrutiny, and risk of reputational harm."

Raymond James, fiscal 2025 10-K (November 2025): the firm says ineffective AI development or deployment could produce "inaccurate output" or biased results. It says it mitigates security and privacy risk with proprietary or "walled-garden" environments, and that AI-related laws "may impose significant operational costs and limit our ability to develop, deploy, or use" AI.

Morgan Stanley, 2025 10-K (February 2026): the firm says new technologies including generative AI and tokenization "will likely continue the pressure on our revenues" in Institutional Securities. It says its Wealth Management competitiveness across advisor-led, workplace and digital direct channels is affected by its technology supporting client needs, including generative AI. It also names threats from generative AI in its cybersecurity program.

Bank of America, 2025 10-K (February 2026): the firm says AI applications that "are not developed and trained properly or contain biases" could cause operational, reputational and financial harm. It says rapid evolution of AI and other emerging technologies could "negatively impact our ability to compete."

FINRA's oversight material (published December 2025) lists effective practices for GenAI. These include ensuring GenAI-assisted customer communications comply with securities laws and FINRA rules, supervising and retaining chatbot communications, and making sure retail communications that mention AI describe how AI is used and balance benefits with risks.

Deloitte (published May 2026) says advisers "will still be the face of the firm," with differentiators of trust, transparency and accountability. It says advisers will need to supervise AI outputs and validate assumptions. It also says agentic AI could extend high-touch planning to a broader client base, while "competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare."

McKinsey (April 2026) projects a shortfall of 90,000 to 110,000 advisors by 2034, which it says makes AI-enabled productivity "a necessary capacity lever." It also argues AI "industrializes the oversight and auditability" once done manually.

Wealthtender consumer survey (August 2025): most respondents were comfortable with AI streamlining admin tasks and somewhat comfortable with AI helping generate personalized plans, but uncomfortable with investment decisions outsourced to AI. The report concludes that "technological enhancement with human oversight represents the future of financial advice."

Capgemini (published June 2026) describes an AI operating model in which AI handles repetitive decisions such as document verification and research summarization, while "humans retain control over critical exceptions to ensure auditability and oversight."

claims.text: Asset-based fees stay dominant, with rates stable rather than falling: McKinsey (published 2025-02-10) says that after fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013 to 2018, fee rates have stabilized, per PriceMetrix by McKinsey. Rates for $1.0 million to $1.5 million relationships have stayed at an average of approximately 104 basis points since 2019.

Pressure expected to be uneven, showing up as transparency and unbundling demands, not a blanket cut: McKinsey (published 2026-04-08) writes that fee rates for relationships of more than $1 million have stayed at about 104 basis points since 2019. It says it anticipates repricing of services where clients see no differentiation, such as basic tax projections. It believes fee pressure will be uneven, "manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points."

Fees could compress as planning gets easier to compare: Deloitte (published 2026-05-20) says lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that execute and maintain pricing. It adds that competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare.

Move from commissions to asset-related fees, with some investors still preferring other models: Cerulli (published 2025-05-28) says that for the past decade financial firms have shifted compensation from largely commission-based to an asset-related fee structure. It reports fee-based payments are preferred by 36% of affluent investors, while some investors still choose commission-based or no-fee services.

Advisor-side revenue models are concentrated in AUM fees, with retainers a minority: the Kitces wellbeing study (published 2023-12-20) found 79% of respondents work in teams that primarily derive client revenue from AUM fees. Another 10% of represented teams were retainer-oriented, and the remainder were mostly hourly or commission.

Consumer-facing guidance lists several models side by side: Wealthtender research (published 2025-08-13) says common models include asset-based fees (typically 0.5% to 1.5% annually), hourly rates ($150-$500+ per hour), flat project fees, or monthly subscription fees.

Large-firm disclosures show asset-based pricing alongside hourly and flat options. The Bank of America 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) states asset management fees are earned as a percentage of AUM and generally range from 50 basis points (bps) to 150 bps. Raymond James's Wealth Advisory Services Program disclosure (published 2026-09-14) says planning fees can be an hourly rate or a fixed (flat) dollar fee. Hourly fees are generally up to $400 per hour, and a percentage fee is not to exceed an annual rate of 2.25% of assets on which investment consulting is provided.

Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management 10-Q (published 2026-08-04) reports asset management and related fees of $1,516 million in the quarter, up 6%. It attributes this to higher average AUM and positive long-term net flows, "partially offset by lower average fee rates, reflecting a change in asset mix." On the 3Q26 call (published 2026-10-14), its CFO said investments across workplace, self-directed and advisory channels increase the funnel and move it "to fee-based."
claims.source_label: MS 10-Q - Wealth Management segment 2026-06-30 [filing]; MS transcript 2026-09-30 [IR]

claims.text: On the 1Q26 call (published 2026-04-22), Raymond James's CEO said the firm wants a "profitable and competitive and fair pricing structure" and would be flexible and open to evolving if the industry moves based on competitive pressures and client preferences. On the 1Q26 call (published 2026-04-16), Schwab's CEO said a service in which Schwab proactively moves cash for clients "is likely an advisory offer, and we charge for advisory offers and would for an agentic advisory offer."

Edward Jones (home firm), in its advisory brochure (published 2026-03-27): every Advisory Solutions Fund Models account pays asset-based fees. That fee "includes a Program Fee and a Platform Fee, less any applicable fee reduction and/or fee offset." It describes the program as suited to clients "comfortable paying monthly, asset-based (percentage) fees for investments and advice rather than individual, transaction-based commissions or sales charges."
claims.source_label: EDJ adv 2026-03-27, p.10 [filing]; EDJ adv 2026-03-27, p.3 [filing]

claims.text: Regulatory baseline is disclosure plus a best-interest standard: FINRA's oversight report (published 2025-12-09) says Reg BI requires broker-dealers not to put their own interests ahead of retail customers when recommending, and "cannot be satisfied through disclosure alone." It also says firms offering services to retail investors must file and provide Form CRS, a plain-language summary that covers fees, conflicts of interest and legal and disciplinary history.

Firms describe the same rules in their filings. The Edward Jones 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says it is subject to Regulation Best Interest and the Form CRS requirement, which covers information on fees, costs and conflicts. The Raymond James 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says implementing these rules led to additional client disclosures and training. It also says various states have proposed or adopted laws that may differ from SEC rules and may lead to additional implementation costs.
claims.source_label: EDJ 10-K 2025-12-31 [filing]; RJF 10-K - Private Client Group segment 2025-09-30 [filing]

claims.text: Regulation has increased price transparency in some markets: the Raymond James 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says that in fixed income and equity markets, regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins.

Firms describe transparency as part of their positioning. Schwab's 2Q26 10-Q (published 2026-08-07) says it aims to offer products "with a focus on transparency, value, and trust" while keeping costs low. Morgan Stanley's advisory brochure (published 2026-11-04) says it endeavors to provide full disclosure of all material facts and will clearly disclose conflicts.

Investors' awareness of fees and disclosures remains limited: the FINRA Investor Education Foundation survey (published 2025-12-04) found 51% of respondents recall receiving disclosures in 2024, versus 59% in 2015. The share who read the entire disclosure fell from 19% to 11%. Also, 20 percent of respondents do not think they pay fees of any kind, and 18 percent do not know how much they pay.
claims.source_label: Research research 2025-12-04, p.25 [research]; Research research 2025-12-04, p.17 [research]

claims.text: Clients say they want transparency: Wealthtender's study (published 2025-08-13) reports 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor. It also reports that lack of fee transparency was identified as a red flag by 38% of survey participants.

Some fees sit outside the headline fee line in disclosures. Morgan Stanley's brochure (published 2026-11-04) says fund fees and expenses are "imbedded in the price of the Fund and, therefore, are not included in the Fee amount in your account statements," with each fund's expense ratio stated in its prospectus. Merrill's brochure (published 2026-10-30) says program-like services may be available at lower or higher fees than the Program Fee, and that the type of account chosen creates a conflict of interest.
claims.source_label: MS adv 2026-11-04, p.26 [filing]; MER adv 2026-10-30, p.54 [filing]

claims.text: Competitors' filings name pricing pressure as a continuing risk. Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) cites lower cost "robo-advice," discount firms, and major competitors that offer zero commissions on stocks, ETFs and other brokerage products. Raymond James's 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says technology has lowered barriers to entry for fintechs, and that direct-to-investor online services or higher deposit rates could result in pricing pressure. Bank of America's 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) cites electronic securities trading with low or no fees and commissions, which may reduce fee-based revenue through pricing pressure. Morgan Stanley's 10-K (published 2026-02-19) says strong competition could lead to pricing pressures that materially adversely affect revenues and profitability.

Digital and low-cost segments are projected to grow fastest: Capgemini's World Wealth Report (published 2026-06-03) projects compounded annual growth in AUM from 2024 to 2030 of 44.1% for the robo advisory market and 6.8% for independent advisors, against about 6.2% for global HNWI AUM. It says digital-first clients prefer robo platforms that deliver low-cost, self-directed experiences.

Client demand is framed as value, not lowest price. Wealthtender (published 2025-08-13) reports pricing is the top factor (48%) in final advisor selection but says this is about demonstrating clear value. McKinsey (published 2025-02-10) says that among investors with more than $1 million in investable assets, the share willing to pay a premium of 100 basis points or more grew by 50 percent from 2021 to 2023.

Platform charges are tied to zero commissions, per trade press (indicative only, not authoritative): a trade-press article (published 2026-09-29) says several sources view platform tolls at large distributors as traceable to the zeroing out of commissions in brokerage. It says the revenue replacement has to come from somewhere if loads aren't charged on funds.

Firms monitor product pricing against competitors. Schwab's 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) says it continually monitors its pricing and periodically adjusts fees for advisory services, expense ratios on mutual funds and ETFs, trade commission rates and other pricing. It names "reduced mutual fund or ETF expense ratios" among forms of price competition that could affect its results.

Revenue sharing and platform payments are disclosed. Schwab's brochure (published 2026-10-15) says it receives compensation from third-party ETF providers for recordkeeping, shareholder and platform services, up to $4 million annually per ETF provider. These can be flat fees, asset-based fees or other negotiated structures, and it does not receive them from Schwab-sponsored ETFs. Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says its other asset-based fee revenue consists of revenue sharing, fund adviser fees, cash solutions and Trust Co. fees.

New third-party fees at Merrill: its Form ADV (published 2026-10-30) says that as of January 1, 2027 it will offer optional data analytics services to certain third-party firms whose products are on its platform. A trade-press article (published 2026-09-29, indicative only) reports two newly created fees, a data analytics fee and a basis-points revenue share costing asset managers as much as 0.1%. It reports data fees of $125,000 to $860,000 per firm per year on actively managed products and $25,000 to $550,000 for passive ETF data. Per that article, Merrill says broker incentives will not shift, but it also states it will have "a financial incentive" to recommend products from firms that pay for data analytics.
claims.source_label: MER adv 2026-10-30, p.61 [filing]; MER trade 2026-09-29 [trade press (indicative only)]

claims.text: Fund share-class and expense-ratio disclosure at Merrill: its brochure (published 2026-10-30) says assets are generally invested in the lowest cost mutual fund share class eligible for the Program. It also says clients should not assume they are in the share class with the lowest possible expense ratio available to the public, and that its money market sweep share class is not necessarily the lowest cost available.

Cash sweep economics are under regulatory and legal scrutiny. A trade-press report (published 2026-10-02, indicative only) says Merrill agreed to pay $39 million to settle a class action over cash sweep interest, on top of a $25 million SEC penalty in January 2025, and that the SEC has focused on cash sweep options since at least 2022. Morgan Stanley's brochure (published 2026-11-04) discloses that sweep banks' income from lending and investing is greater than the fees earned from money market funds available as a sweep investment.
claims.source_label: MER trade 2026-10-02 [trade press (indicative only)]; MS adv 2026-11-04, p.29 [filing]

claims.text: Unbundling is the signpost McKinsey (published 2026-04-08) tells firms to watch. Its questions ask what signposts, including "sustained unbundling," will show whether the bear case is materializing.

Edward Jones (home firm), in its advisory brochure (published 2026-03-27): its Advisory Solutions Fund Models Fee includes a Program Fee and a Platform Fee. ETFs, affiliated mutual funds and unaffiliated mutual funds in the account carry internal fees and expenses described in each fund's prospectus. It also states that when a client takes a Reserve Line advance rather than withdrawing money from the account, Edward Jones retains the fee those assets generate and receives revenue from the lender.

claims.text: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says the Partnership's ability to compete and adapt may be adversely affected by generational wealth transfer, including "changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values." The filing does not break these preferences out by age group.

Cerulli research (published 2025-10-29) states that "older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives." This is industry research, not an Edward Jones disclosure.

The Bank of America Private Bank 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (published 2026-06-17) reports that 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets, and 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios. 65% still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor. This is a wealthy-American sample from another firm's study, not Edward Jones clients.

The Bank of America Private Bank 2024 Study of Wealthy Americans (published 2024-06-18) says Millennials and Gen Z allocate three times more of their portfolios to alternative investments than older generations. For ages 21-43, the greatest-opportunity picks include real estate investments (31%), crypto/digital assets (28%) and private equity (26%), and 21% chose companies focused on positive impact. This is a wealthy-American sample, not Edward Jones clients.

Cerulli research (published 2025-10-29) states that Millennials (ages 27-42) will inherit more over the next 25 years ($46 trillion) than Generation X households. Gen X stands to inherit the greater portion in the next 10 years, $14 trillion to Millennials' $8 trillion.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says the Partnership is making substantial investments in initiatives to meet clients' planning, investing, saving, spending, borrowing and comprehensive needs. It names recently launched Financial Planning Services, which gives clients "a more personalized experience with additional planning capabilities." It also names three client-targeting initiatives: High Net Worth, Workplace, and "a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors." The firm adds that it "cannot reliably predict the timing or outcome" of these initiatives.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) describes the Digital and Data division as supporting investment in technology infrastructure and digital initiatives. Management says branch teams use new tools "for deeper discovery conversations with clients and more comprehensive advice and planning."

InvestmentNews (published 2026-08-18, trade press, indicative only) reports that Edward Jones took a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken. The stated intention is to integrate Quicken's personal financial management capabilities into Edward Jones to support its value proposition and advisor conversations. The same article says Edward Jones is still determining the deployment strategy, including where and how Quicken will be offered to clients. The article does not tie this to younger clients.

WealthManagement.com (published 2026-09-30, trade press, indicative only) reports that Edward Jones is developing an end-to-end retirement plan management tool with Aboon and Retirement Plan Advisory Group, to help advisors serve business owners and their employees. The prospecting module is in beta with advisors and is expected to go live to the broader network early next year. This relates to the Workplace initiative, not to a younger-client offering specifically.

On the 10-Q for the period ended 2025-06-27 (published 2025-08-08), management said net new assets fell 10% in the second quarter and 8% in the first half of 2025. It attributed the decline to higher outflows, impacted by factors including "an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm." It said the decrease was attributable to existing clients.

On the 10-Q for the period ended 2025-09-26 (published 2025-11-07), management said net new assets decreased 4% in the first nine months of 2025. It cited elevated outflows, "partially offset by stronger inflows," and again named an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm among the factors.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) lists "competition for clients and personnel in light of the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, changing client demographics, preferences and values" among its most notable strategic risks. It says the firm addresses them through initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact for current and potential clients.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says the Partnership faces competition from robo-advisors and other lower cost options, and from "fintech" companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms. It adds that "If the Partnership does not meet client needs, the Partnership could lose clients, thereby reducing revenues and profitability." It also says major competitors offer zero commissions on stock, ETF and other brokerage purchases and sales, usually with lower levels of personalized service. The filing does not tie this competition to younger investors specifically.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) describes the firm's response as significant investments in financial advisors, human capital, technology infrastructure, digital initiatives, knowledge- and data-powered tools and strategic relationships. It also names the new digital platform focused on Next Generation investors.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) names risks tied to the digital response. Increased cost from digital initiatives "may continue to adversely impact the Partnership's profitability." Fraud exposure is expected to increase as new digital tools and client-facing technologies are deployed.

On the 10-Q for the period ended 2026-03-27 (published 2026-05-07), management said communications and data processing expense rose 19% to $317 in the first quarter of 2026, "primarily due to continued investments in new tools and technology."

The evidence above only provides objective context for the strategic question asked. Whether or how Edward Jones should act is a judgment for the strategy team to make, beyond the scope of this evidence engine.
